data.title: Design the Definition API from DMG, fields and the data-tools Dream Code
data.description:
Why: the proposal's §8.1 Dialect(...) sketch was never built; both existing Dialects are hand-written data plus hand-written builders. Everything else in M3 is shaped by this API, so it is designed from three data points before any of it is built.

What: a dated design doc under project/ (and a hand-written sketch of each of the three Dialects as Definition API calls, as pseudocode checked for expressiveness) that says: what a Dialect declares (types, number type, Iteration Spaces, intrinsics with each target's spelling and a reference implementation, a Library, targets with their compare mode, size flags, declared purity and effects); what a Grammar declares (constructs, slots of three kinds, fragments); how the generated builder reports errors; where a slot in another language (SQL) fits; and what from the M2 findings' "What M3 should change" is in or out. Settle the two decisions in it that the plan names (program DAG; foreign slots) or raise them for Ben.

Already decided: the tolerance rule (one declared figure plus a per-case override with a reason); Dialects are nominally typed; Dialects import by namespace with named interface types at the seam (the composition note's B-with-C, a recommendation, not built, so this leaf says whether v0 includes it); Dream Code before Dialect.

Seams: reads kit/dialects/dmg, kit/dialects/fields, kit/lower/environment.d.ts and the Dream Code. Writes only a doc. The doc compares every Environment field with its Definition API call and lists any field the API cannot express.

Out of scope: building any of it.

Open questions for Ben: the program DAG and foreign-slot decisions, if the evidence does not settle them.

The data-tools Dream Code's ten examples are each placed against the API, with the gaps named

data.title: Decision: is the program DAG part of the kit core?
data.description:
Question: the data-tools Dream Code has a DAG of tables, params, charts and views, with lineage and "what reruns when a param moves". The DMG's Game and a field's params are also structures above the Kernels. Should the kit own one generic graph IR, with the query API answering lineage questions over it, or should each Dialect keep its own structure?

Options: (a) a small generic graph IR in the kit, which Dialects instantiate; (b) per-Dialect structures, with the query API covering Kernels only; (c) a graph IR in the kit only when a second Dialect needs it.

What waits on it: the query and pass API's scope, and the data-tools Grammar. Needs the design leaf's evidence first.

data.title: Decision: how the SQL plugin runs
data.description:
Question: the Dream Code's SQL component needs a parser (for spans and schema inference), a checker, and an engine to run the query.

Options: (a) a hand-written SQL subset (select, join, where, group by, order by, limit, a few functions): no dependency, spans and schemas for free, real work, never SQLite; (b) an embedded engine such as sql.js (wasm): real SQL, a dependency and a large blob in a one-page artifact (check the M0 platform findings for what a page can fetch); (c) (a) for checking and inference, (b) for execution.

Project rule: avoid dependencies; ask before adding one. What waits on it: the data-tools Dialect's SQL slot.

data.title: Decision: the capture policy for build-time values
data.description:
Question: real DSL code closes over build-time values (`row[column]`, `q[lo]`, `bucket`, `user`, `at`), as the Dream Code's fragments and `cohort` component do. The Runtime Subset rejects free variables and dynamic property names (proposal §5.5); M1 counted captures (11 of 126 DMG lambdas use a top-level helper) and rejected them with L001.

Options: (a) explicit build-time bindings: the construct passes named constants into the lambda's environment, and a reference to anything else stays L001; (b) specialization: a lambda is lowered after the build-time values are substituted as constants, so `row[column]` with a known `column` becomes a field access; (c) refuse closures and let authors write the column name literally, with a fixit.

Why it matters: it decides whether fragments like `winsorize` and components like `cohort` can have runtime lambdas at all, and so how expressive Grammars can be. The design leaf proposes; this leaf records Ben's choice. Evidence first: how many Dream Code lambdas need it (the design leaf counts).

data.title: The program record: declarations as a uniform node list in the kit core
data.description:
Why: proposal §5.2 puts "Declarations: generic nodes for whatever the dialect's grammar declares, each pointing at its kernels" in the core; it was never built. The kit carries three parallel hand-written versions (DMG's declarations and lambda slots, fields' Program, the signatures lowering returns). Addresses, the graph view, the agent's `ir()`, the generated language reference and the dependency query all need one uniform node list.

What: a small program record in the kit core: a list of nodes, each with an id, a construct kind, its declared data, a span, a phase (build or run) and the Kernels it owns, in a stable JSON form with a listing. A Dialect fills it in; the kit does not know what the kinds mean. Edges are not stored: the dependency query (the query leaf) derives them from Kernel effects on declared places plus edges a Dialect declares for its non-Kernel nodes. DMG, fields and the data Dialect are three clients.

Already decided: the reviewer's reading, adopted as the working direction: declaration table in the kit; edges derived; execution and reactivity (rerun on a param move, caching, frame loops) are a Dialect's, not the core's (proposal §5.3 and §9.1). Not a generic DAG: DMG's graph is cyclic and a field's is a star.

Seams: kit/ir (new record type and verifier rule), kit/lower. Existing DMG and fields output must not change. Out of scope: a typed dataflow layer between nodes (build it only if a Dialect needs kit-checked values flowing between nodes; see the composition note).

data.title: Kit boundary, check, and a generic differential harness
data.description:
Why: H5 says the agent should not need kit source, which is measurable only if its work lives outside kit/ against a public import surface. The proposal's §11 has a layout, a check loop (`node kit/check.js`, at most 40 lines, every diagnostic with a code and a fix) and budgets enforced by tests; the plan had none of them. A fresh agent's Dialect also needs a generic way to run its Kernels through the interpreter and the emitted JS on sample inputs; kit/harness today runs only fields Programs, and the same differential gate is what H11's passes need.

What: (1) a kit boundary: Dialects live outside kit/ (move the three), and kit exports one documented surface; (2) `check`: one command that loads a Dialect and its programs and prints every diagnostic with a code, a span and a fix, and runs the verifier; (3) a generic differential harness, a library that takes any Dialect's Kernels, inputs and targets and compares them (the fields harness becomes one client); (4) the budget tests the proposal describes, for the docs' token size.

Seams: kit/harness, kit/dialects/*, package layout. Risk: moving Dialects out of kit/ touches every import; do it in one commit with the type check as the gate.

data.title: Emit SQL from table pipelines (optional, late)
data.description:
Optional, late. Proposal §6 names SQL a target plugin: something a Dialect compiles to. If the data Dialect's table operators are in place, emit a SQL SELECT from a table pipeline, golden-tested, with no engine and no dependency, so the data domain has a second backend as fields has JS and GLSL.

Why: it is the cheap way to test "one source drives two outputs" over tables, and it matches the proposal's meaning. It is not needed for H2, H4, H5 or H11. Do it only if the earlier leaves leave time, or the fresh-agent runs need a second backend to exercise. Out of scope: running SQL, parsing SQL (Ben ruled it is not an input).

data.title: Queries over Kernels and the program record
data.description: Why: Manuel's advice was inspection APIs first, and read-only queries need no Definition API: who writes a place, what a loop's body reads, def-use, reaching stores, and one dependency query fed by Kernel effects on declared places plus edges a Dialect declares for non-Kernel nodes (so 'downstream of a param' and 'who reads param k' are one query). The kit already hand-rolls pieces: kit/emit/glsl/capabilities.js looks through helpers for purity, and the verifier collects effects. Their answers are the evidence the program-record decision rests on. What: a small query library over Kernels and the program record, with tests on DMG and fields Kernels. Out of scope: passes (the pass manager leaf).

data.text:
REVISION 2026-11-24, after an independent Fable design review and Ben's rulings (SQL is not an input language; Dream Code may be rejected with errors and fixits). The design doc must also settle or carry:
1. Build against DMG first: write a throwaway EXECUTABLE DMG definition that reproduces dmgEnvironment for one hard preset (10 or 14), checked by deep equality over its slot refs, because pseudocode is weak protection for keyed slots, emit, inferred methods, list.with and drawResult unions. Fields is the cheap confirmation, not the first.
2. Split the API into a static part (types, intrinsics, Library, targets) and a program-shaped part (constructs to Environment and program record). An Environment cannot exist without a Program's declarations, so a Dialect half and a Grammar half cut through DMG's index.js, which is mostly that derivation.
3. Lambda kinds are four, not three: declaration; build-time lambda (async, may read data such as schemas and samples, returns more grammar, not constants: proposal §5.4 needs a correction); runtime Kernel lambda; host-JS lambda re-run when a param moves (`.title(() => ...)`, the proposal's browser-only state). Say how the API names each.
4. The capture policy for build-time values is a decision (leaf cfUzUl); count how many Dream Code lambdas need it.
5. A Dialect declares its own effect verbs: EffectVerb in kit/ir/ir.d.ts is a closed union of DMG verbs (sfx, toast, hud, spawn, destroy, end, rng). The core is still game-shaped there.
6. An integer value type and null semantics: the core has neither (numberType is f32|f64). Decide whether the data Dialect gets them or rejects what it cannot type (count(), LIMIT, dropNulls, units: int). Integers are also what M5's hostless backend needs.
7. Lambdas as source strings (fields) or functions via String(fn) (DMG, the Dream Code): the generated builder must pick one.
8. Where the tolerance lives: declare it in the Dialect's target declaration (proposal §8.1), not in kit/emit/glsl.
9. Rename one of: the live-session 'Environment' in the Dream Code, and the glossary's Environment (what lowering resolves against).
10. State H2's failure condition now: fails if data-specific logic lands in kit/ir or kit/lower, or if DMG or fields output moves. Also state what fraction of the data Dialect's meaning the IR carries (groupBy, join, agg and sort are not Kernels).
11. Reject-with-fixit policy: the Dream Code's layout inside programs (contradicts G3), Vega-Lite encodings, agent permissions, a global fragment registry, pivot/describe/winsorize breadth, async data reads beyond schema and sample, and program-editing mutations (addStep, toProgram; those are the lab API, M4) are not kit features. Each gets a diagnostic with a fixit where an author could write them, or is simply out.
12. The Dream Code's builder operators the SQL rewrite invented (Builder gaps): year/date parts, join with {on, take}, sort("-col"), semiJoin, keepGroups. They are the data Dialect's, not the kit's.
13. Fragments scoped to a Dialect or program, not a global registry. Dialect imports (composition note) are OUT of v0.

REFRAMED 2026-11-24. The question 'is the program DAG in the core' bundled three things: (1) the declaration table: yes, in the kit (proposal §5.2 already promised it; leaf RJtpuF); (2) edges: derived from Kernel effects on declared places plus edges a Dialect declares for non-Kernel nodes, not stored, and not a DAG (DMG is cyclic, a field is a star); (3) execution and reactivity (rerun on param move, caching, frames): a Dialect's, not the core's. The design leaf and the query leaf (dynUhe) supply evidence; this leaf is Ben's confirmation. Evidence that would change the reading: toward less, if the three program records share nothing beyond id, kind and span (then the kit owns only a nodes()/edges() interface); toward more, if a second domain needs typed values flowing between nodes with kit-checked types (the composition note's gaps 2 and 3); toward a shared relational stage, if table operators must reach a second backend.

REVISION 2026-11-24. No SQL slot: SQL is not an input language (the Dream Code was rewritten in the builder; see its Builder gaps). Accept the data Dialect's pure runtime lambdas and its table operators. Be honest about H2: the Dream Code's lambdas are all pure, so this Dialect does NOT exercise effects or stores; it presses on an integer value type, null semantics and captured build-time values, and most of its meaning (groupBy, agg, join, sort) is not Kernels at all. The findings must say what fraction of the Dialect the IR carries. Dream Code that the kit does not build is rejected with a diagnostic and a fixit, or left out; record which.

data.description:
Why: Ben's ruling (2026-11-24, now an AGENTS.md rule): whenever an agent is asked to use something we made, a few fresh agents use it and report before the design is locked in. Here the thing is the Definition API's draft, and the task is mapping the data-tools Dream Code onto it. How hard the mapping is, is the feedback on the Dialect API. No need to build the API first.

What: from the design leaf's output, write (1) a strict rule set for the conversion, checkable by a program where possible (a checker script in scripts/ that loads a candidate Dialect and prints every violation with a code and a fix: required declarations present, no f64 mixing, every Dream Code lambda either lowers or is rejected with a diagnostic, every rejected feature has a stated reason), and (2) the draft API as documentation only (the design doc's API section plus a small worked example, the DMG or fields definition, written in the draft). Give each of 3 fresh agents (say which model; the subject is models) only the rules, the draft API and the Dream Code, and have each convert it to a Dialect (and Grammar as far as the draft allows) written against the draft. Then review each result by hand. Record, per agent: tokens read, what they had to guess, what they asked for that the draft lacks, where the rules misled them, what they refused to map and why, and how much massage the output needed to pass the checker.

Already decided: the data Dialect has no SQL slot (SQL is not an input language); the Dream Code is a probe, and what the kit will not build is rejected with a diagnostic and a fixit; lambdas of the data Dialect are pure, so it does not test effects.

What this changes: the findings go into the design doc as marked corrections, and the Definition API leaf builds the revised design, not the first draft. If the agents converge on a different shape than the draft, the draft changes; if they diverge, the API has too many ways to say one thing.

Out of scope: building the API; the fresh-agent runs from START.md, API.md and hello (a later leaf, on another domain).

data.description: DECISION for Ben. Found in iJtvVE (4a640f7): kit/define's generated const convention forbids every effect (as DMG's does), so a fields constant can no longer call a helper; the hand-written fields Dialect allowed it. data.text:
Blind-pass design written: project/2026-11-24-architecture-consult-design.md (criterion ITS).

Recommendation in brief:
- At workbench scale the complexity moves out of optimizers and linkers and into four places: capturing behavior, defining dialects, the seams between them, and legibility. Optimization becomes scheduling and caching inside each dialect.
- Keep JS DSLs, our own parser, one typed IR, our own emitters, no embedded engine. Change four things: (1) parse whole program files, not only String(fn), for exact closure capture and spans; (2) the core IR is for behavior (kernels) only, and structure stays per-dialect data with addresses; (3) runtime values in structure get no special form: build-time param reads are plain values, tracked and rebuilt on change, and only cross-part signals need a kernel; (4) composition is a kit service: parts are processes with clocks, only signals (snapshots) and kernels cross, plus one lab: address scheme, a scheduler, and frame tags checked at crossings.
- Dialect = immutable builder classes + TS-like sig strings + slot markers (Build, Native, Kernel, GpuKernel) + engine + view + a required text(). Types flow because kernels are typed eagerly at the builder call.
- Worked example: Lantern Cave (cave + arcade + fields + tables), 61 lines, ~0.9–1.2k tokens.
- Top risks: capture rules versus natural code; one-pass dialect authoring from the docs alone; composition semantics. Each has a 0.5–2 day experiment in §7.
- Correction to the brief §6: Jig's L0–L6 are views computed from one compile, not successive lowerings.

I've written `design.md` beside the brief. It's about 9,800 words, longer than the 20-minute target (more like 25 minutes, much of it tables), with depth in appendices. Facts are tagged by how I know them: read in code, measured with a script over `inputs/`, or inferred. I ran nothing from Jig.

## Summary of the recommendation

Keep programs in JavaScript, but split them by when code runs. Code that runs once at build time stays ordinary JS, run natively, and the fluent builders record a graph of domain nodes. Any lambda that re-runs (on a parameter change, every tick) or runs per element (per cell, pixel or row) is written in **Kernel JS**: a strict subset of JS syntax with the kit's meaning. In Kernel JS, vector operators work, units and frames are type-checked, and `u8` state fields wrap.

The kit reads these lambdas with `String(fn)` and parses them. It looks up their free names among the module's top-level bindings, so helpers and constants just work, which is the one real advantage tracing has. It keeps natural operators and real `if`/loops, which tracing loses.

Kernel JS lowers into one small typed core for **behavior** only. A kit-owned reference interpreter fixes its meaning; it compiles to JS closures by default, GLSL/WGSL per pixel, and C for export. **Structure** goes into a graph typed by each DSL's schema, not into that core.

DSLs compose through typed ports. What crosses a port is one of about a dozen shared **seam types** (grid, mesh, signal, field and so on), each carrying unit, frame, identity space and clock. Code can cross too: one helper runs in JS at build time in one DSL and in GLSL in another, which ends the hand-duplicated shaders.

To define a DSL, a model writes a schema (about 700 tokens for a game DSL like DMG's), plus a reference runtime and views (I estimate 6–12k tokens). The kit derives the builder, checker, reference, completions, parameter panel and agent help from the schema. The worked example in the doc is a procedurally generated cave, played in a tile-game DSL and lit by a GPU lighting DSL, with seam errors shown in full.

## Old world vs new world

Keep the old world's semantics machinery and drop its machinery for scale and speed:

- **Carries over:** a typed core, staging (binding times), one IR read many ways, names as identity with provenance, dialects defined as data, legality per target, differential testing.
- **Dead weight:** SSA/CFG optimizers, separate compilation, incremental invalidation, lossless syntax trees, rich type systems.
- **New:** a language definition small enough for a model to write in one go, seams that are about meaning (millimetres vs metres, per frame vs per pixel), and tokens-to-correct as the cost to minimize.

Your suspicion holds but misses its upstream half. All three systems I read fail at the same spot: getting hold of runtime lambdas. Binding time is the concept that unifies seams, staging and "runtime values inside structure".

## Three biggest risks

Each has a one-to-two-day experiment in the doc, with a kill criterion.

1. **Kernel JS friction.** Models may keep writing outside the subset. On the evidence so far, a scan of DMG's 113 runtime lambdas found about four in five already inside it, and about one in ten reaching top-level helpers or constants.
2. **The schema layer costs more than it saves**, or forces real domains into `t.any` escape hatches.
3. **Seam types buy no real leverage** once DSLs are actually composed.

## Questions for you

1. Will DSL runtimes stay model-written per workbench, or come from a kit library of reusable runtimes?
2. Is composition within one workbench, or across workbenches by importing a published DSL?
3. Is C export a requirement or a demo?
4. What edit-to-run latency do you want? I assumed under 100 ms, excluding heavy domain compute.
5. When the DSL changes, should old programs be migrated, or just re-checked with presets as the regression suite?
6. Which small models, and do they have tool use?
7. Is checkJs meant to check programs, or only the kit's own code?
8. Do you have an evaluation yardstick the experiments should use?

## Where I think the brief is wrong

- **§1's list of hard problems leaves out getting hold of behavior and binding time.** Both come before seams, legibility and verification.
- **"One small typed core IR" is right for behavior and wrong for structure.** Forcing tile maps, B-rep timelines or tables into it would distort them.
- **`String(fn)` alone drops the values a lambda closes over.** Jig's cache key has exactly this gap: `hash.js` keys functions by `fn.toString()`.
- **G-verify overpromises.** We can show the fast backends agree with the reference interpreters. We can't show a model-written reference runtime means what the user intended.
- **checkJs as the checker for programs conflicts with C-browser**, because the TypeScript compiler is several MB to run in the page. It's fine for the kit's own code.
- **"The DSLs are JavaScript" needs a qualifier:** code that runs later or per element should be Kernel JS.
- **Two chapters of *Uncommon Math* are shorter than 94k characters** (34,884 and 57,034). The book's other figures check out.

I couldn't verify in an artifact whether `new Function` survives the CSP, or whether WebGPU is available. DMG and Jig both use `new Function`, and each is a 10-minute probe.

Jig is cloned in `jig/`. My scratch copies of the example files are in `../consult-scratch/`.

data.title: Module-scope scan: line terminators, regex/template flips and quadratic time (review of c189880)
data.description:
Why: the module-scope scan (kit/parse/blank.js, toplevel.js) is what a Definition API host uses to vouch for a top-level helper (B012). A misread can make a closure pass as a helper that reads the wrong binding, silently: the one outcome that must never happen. Three review rounds running (04567fb, c2845ca, c189880) found a high bug of this kind. Review of c189880 by reviewer-scan, 2026-11-24; probes in local/rev-c189880-probes/ (lineterm, label, lexer, perf, fuzz.mjs, fuzz-guard.mjs, corpus.mjs).

Findings, all confirmed by probe:
1. HIGH: a line comment, a regex and an unclosed string end only at \n, not \r, U+2028 or U+2029, so code after one is hidden from the scan. An end-to-end probe builds a helper whose lowered body reads top-level k = 100 while the real function multiplies by 3. Nothing reports it.
2. HIGH as a class: any wrong regex-vs-division guess whose misread span holds a backtick flips template text and code for the rest of the file, so a declaration inside a template looks top-level and the real one disappears. ScanError fires only on a duplicate. Confirmed: a label after a statement with no ';' or after `if (a)` (c189880's label fix is incomplete). Also misread: `export default /re/`, `extends /re/`, `1./2`, `++/re/.lastIndex`. A balance guard (a closer that closes nothing, brackets open at EOF, odd backticks) catches both end-to-end probes and refuses none of 518 corpus files, but the fuzzer found one case where two flips cancel out.
3. MEDIUM: toplevel.js is quadratic. declaration() calls lineEnds at each newline and re-slices the text per whitespace character: 20k newlines in a comment inside a declaration take 6.1 s, 80k take 102 s.
4. LOW: `const f = (x) => x` followed by a line starting `{` runs init into the block, so B012 refuses a valid helper (fails safe).

The README's "known misreads" are not harmless: each is a way to a wrong helper. The TypeScript-parser oracle (local/rev-c2845ca-probes/oracle.mjs) should become a kept test either way: corpus plus cases in the fast suite, a seeded fuzz in prerelease asserting never a fake top-level name and never a wrong const init.

Decision for Ben: keep patching the hand lexer (fix 1, the keyword and label gaps, add the balance guard and the oracle tests), or replace blank.js and toplevel.js with a real JavaScript parser (acorn: about 120 KB, MIT, no dependencies, runs in the page; a new dependency, which needs Ben's approval).

criteria.label: The end-to-end probes in local/rev-c189880-probes (lineterm, label) refuse or read correctly, as kept tests
The TypeScript-parser oracle runs over the corpus in the fast suite and as a seeded fuzz in prerelease

Lowering refuses any other effect with a fixit. Reuse the IR's effect kinds (kit/ir/README.md: read, write, rng, emit, call) and the DMG lowering's store rules (kit/lower) rather than inventing new ones; say what the IR already carries and what it lacks. Include how the particles sheet would be written with it, as a sketch, and the rules a checker can enforce.

Open: whether spawn is a verb in a lambda or a component's own job (an emitter's rate); whether a write to own members needs per-member permission. The draft agent's call, stated with the reason; anything architectural goes to Ben.

data.title: kit/define: the review lows on within, bounds and required (aa80fb3)
data.description:
Why: the review of aa80fb3 (reviewer-within, 2026-11-24) found nothing serious, and seven lows on one surface. Probes in local/rev-aa80fb3-probes/ (within, bounds, required, nested-name, lower-ids .probe.js; run with node <path> from the repo root).

What, each confirmed by probe:
1. An opening name scoped within its own construct (account opens name("account", { within: "account" })) is accepted, and its uniqueness is never checked: each instance is its own scope. Make it D011 (within.probe.js case 4).
2. data("number", { min: 0 }) accepts Infinity, and { max: 10 } accepts -Infinity. Ruling (main thread, 2026-11-24): a bounded number is finite, as host param values already must be; refuse with B004.
3. A bound set no value can satisfy (min 0.5, max 0.6, whole) is accepted; only min > max is D011. Make an empty whole range D011 too.
4. required: false on the root gives D011 saying "is required but has no parent"; fix the message.
5. an() picks the article by first letter only ("an user", "an unit", "an one"). A small rule for the common cases is enough.
6. Doc gap that bites the stateful run: a stateful construct cannot reuse a scoped name across instances (the state namespace stays Program-wide, so stateOf could not tell them apart; within.probe.js case 5a). Say so in API.md's within sentence.
7. Doc gap: kit/define/README.md's "Ref ids" paragraph names two ways two instances share a name; within adds a third (handled by the ~2 guard; lower-ids.probe.js).

Seams: kit/define/validate-grammar.js, shapes.js, codes.js, README.md, kit/API.md (keep it short).

data.text: sheet-writer: drafted scripts/particles/docs/dream-code.md (worktree agent-ae881bcef69a5fd35) with 20 refusals, plus scripts/particles/README.md. Choices stated in the sheet: no spawn verb in lambdas (emitters are the only source); spawn may not kill; rng only directly in spawn; force writes vel only; no lambda writes age; whole-field writes only (p.vel.x = 0 refused); helpers are pure. Not yet through its blind readers.

REVISED 2026-11-24 (main thread, from Ben's question on system, network and graphics calls): the draft must also cover effects on intrinsics. Today every intrinsic is assumed pure ("no member can carry an effect", kit/define/README.md), so once slots allow effects, a Dialect could declare an I/O intrinsic and a pure slot could call it unseen. Draft: an intrinsic declares its effect kinds (none means pure); lowering adds them to the call's effects, as a method call's already include its callee's; each slot's allowed effects gate intrinsic calls too. Async never enters a lambda: network and long-running calls are request values the host runs (both app-DSL designs converge on this), so a request builder is pure. API.md must say plainly that the Dialect author vouches for each intrinsic's declared effects, since the kit cannot inspect a ref. Also from the app-DSL probe: shared state needs a fourth category beside pure, own-instance and commutative/run-once, a per-key ordered log (an outbox); say whether the draft includes it or parks it.

REVISED 2026-11-24 (from Ben's question "if the DSL has .play('song.mid'), who writes play so we can generate wasm or C?"): today an intrinsic's spelling is a per-target code template and there is no host interface, so a retargeted effectful intrinsic means hand-written glue per Dialect per target. Proposal for the draft, to confirm with Ben: an effectful intrinsic is a declared host import (name, type, effect kinds); its spelling on every target is "call import <name>". From the declared imports the kit generates the C header, the wasm import table, the JS host interface (.d.ts) and a recording stub for the reference interpreter, so the differential harness compares the sequence of host calls across targets without real I/O. The platform host library (WebAudio, SDL, the DMG runtime) stays hand-written by whoever builds that host. A build-time builder method (.music("song.mid")) is a fact in the Program record that the host reads, with no codegen. Particles needs almost none of this; settle the shape in the draft anyway. See project/2026-11-24-app-dsl-probe.md: both app designs describe host calls as data.

RULED 2026-11-24 (Ben): agents define host implementations somewhere, never handwaved, and may do it either way. (1) Net-new host code in the kit's own language (the glossary's Runtime Subset; a short name is pending, Ben's call), lowered, checked against its declared effects and portable to every backend: the Library grown from helpers into host modules. (2) A foreign module, a packaged JS file with a declared interface (names, types, effect kinds), trusted rather than lowered, accepted only by targets that can host it (JS; wasm in the page via imports; never GLSL; not C). Main-thread proposal for the draft: an import has an implementation per target, a Runtime Subset one counting for all; a Program using an import with no implementation for a target gets a capability refusal naming it. The reference interpreter calls a foreign JS module directly, so the differential harness still compares JS and wasm. Precedent: local/form-skate-workbench.html's Form.plugin (install($, ir) declares systems with .phase, .reads(places), .writes(places), .tick; createWorld returns the one host object that owns shared state; a Program composes plugins with $.use). Its World is arbitrary JS, hence JS-only: the gap this ruling closes. Backlog candidate: an embedded JS engine (QuickJS) so C can host a foreign module.
